newsitem.title: PERU: Peru refuses to release prisoners in hostage drama.
newsitem.headline: Peru refuses to release prisoners in hostage drama.

text.p: Peru's government refused on Friday to release jailed comrades of leftist guerrillas who held nearly 400 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence for a third day.

An emergency meeting of ministers agreed, "to approve the proposal of the President (Alberto Fujimori) not to accept the demand to release any terrorists held in Peru's jails," according to a statement read by a Government Palace official.
The hostages -- including diplomats, foreign businessmen and government officials -- were believed to be one of the largest and highest-ranking group of people ever held captive, experts said.

The men, still clad in elegant clothes they wore for the cocktail party the rebels stormed on Tuesday, spent another uncomfortable night on the floor of the home, making do with meagre food and water.

Tentative negotiations with the rebels have produced no apparent progress although four dazed hostages, one needing a wheelchair, were released late Thursday and about 100 women and elderly have been freed since the start of the siege.

Japan said sharp differences existed over the handling of the siege following a one-hour emergency meeting in Lima between Fujimori and Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who arrived Thursday to help with negotiations.
"Japan and Peru are far apart in ideas," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said. He did not elaborate on the problem, but said it was hampering progress toward a solution.
As the embassy residence is legally on Japanese territory, Fujimori would in theory need Tokyo's approval for any assault.
Fujimori, facing the most serious crises of his political career, promised in a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton that the safety of hostages would be his first priority in resolving the siege.

"I am occupying myself permanently and jointly with my team to achieve a solution as soon as possible to this crisis, the principal objective being the safeguarding of the health and life of those who are inside," he wrote in the letter.
Fujimori, who ignored an ultimatum by the rebels for his presence Wednesday, has still not made a public statement since the crisis began.
In the street outside the residence, crowds held a candle- lit vigil through the night.
"There are 24 million Peruvians who will not allow the lives of those kidnapped to be threatened," said one of the vigil organisers, legislator Manuel Lajo.
A Spanish comedian, Francisco Carbonell, even offered to enter the compound and tell jokes to ease the tension.

Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent, released late Tuesday with three other diplomats to mediate between rebels and authorities outside, said conditions in the residence, normally home to six people, were very cramped. "They're packed in," he said.
Red Cross official Juan Pedro Schaerer, however, said: "The hostages are well. Nobody is sick." He added that rebels had given the hostages permission to write letters to relatives.
The Red Cross supplied the captives with water, some food, medical supplies and even chess sets and rosary chains. The organisation said 380 hostages were left inside.
Governments worldwide have urged Peru not to use force and to do everything in its power to protect the hostages.

The United States on Thursday sent a team of security advisers to Lima to assist the U.S. ambassador to Peru in the crisis, the State Department said. The ambassador and his deputy attended the reception, but left before the siege.

The rebels assaulted the fortified compound from outside on Tuesday, linking up with comrades disguised as waiters inside a cocktail reception to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday, anti-terrorist police sources said. Cartridges were smuggled into the building beforehand among flowers and inside a Christmas cake.

The rebels released Fujimori's mother and sister, but were still believed to be holding one of his brothers. The president, the son of Japanese immigrants, apparently had planned to attend the party but was delayed on a trip to the provinces.
The captives also include Peru's foreign minister, agriculture minister, supreme court president and the current and past chiefs of the anti-terrorism police.
Ecuador, which fought a brief border war with Peru early 1995, offered asylum to the rebels.
"We can be of help, providing the Peruvian government asks for it," Ecuadoran President Abdala Bucaram said.
Attempts by the MRTA and the previously better-known Shining Path to overthrow the government have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
